title: In the entrance exam, calculate the right side first and then attach it to the left side.
when_to_show: When you see code like `x = x + 1`,
body: When reading an assignment statement, calculate the expression on the right side first, rather than trying to memorize the name on the left. For example, `x = x + 1` works by reading the existing value of `x`, adding 1 to it, and then assigning the result back to the variable `x`. So, if `x` was 2, after execution, `x` becomes 3. Beginners may find it strange that `x` appears on both sides simultaneously, but you can think of the `x` on the right as the previous value and the `x` on the left as the name where the new value will be stored. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather a reading guide designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the variable’s initial value, the value after assignment, the result of a condition, changes during a loop, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When you’re confused, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; start by noting whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. In an assignment statement, the right-hand side is evaluated first and then assigned to the variable on the left. A line like `x = x + 1` reads the existing value of `x`, adds 1 to it, and then stores the result back into `x`. When reading code, you must distinguish between the value before assignment and the value after assignment. If a variable is assigned a value multiple times, the value stored last is used in subsequent lines.
detail: In an assignment statement, the flow is not to read the left-hand side first, but to calculate the value on the right-hand side and then store the result in the left-hand side. In `x = x + 1`, the `x` on the right-hand side is the previous value, and the `x` on the left-hand side is the name that will hold the new value. If the same variable is assigned a value multiple times, subsequent lines use the value that was last stored.

title: The "print" line determines the value displayed on the screen.
body: In problems involving output results, you’re often asked what value appears on the screen at the end. Even if a value is stored in a variable, it won’t appear on the screen unless you use `print`. Conversely, if a calculation is included inside a `print` statement, the result of that calculation appears immediately on the screen. `print(x + 1)` is not code that changes `x` itself; rather, it reads the value of `x`, adds 1, and displays the result. Always read storage and output separately. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather a reading exercise designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial value of a variable, the value after assignment, the result of a condition, changes during a loop, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. A `print` statement determines the value displayed on the screen. However, `print` does not store a value or return a function result. When reading code, you must distinguish between the value printed to the screen and the value retained in the variable. Also, note that if a function contains only `print` statements and no `return` statement, the result of the call may be `None`.
detail: `print` is a command that displays a value on the screen, not one that stores it. `print(x + 1)` prints the result of the calculation without changing `x`. When reading code, you must distinguish between the value remaining in the variable and the value displayed on the screen. If a function contains only `print` and no `return` statement, the result of the call may be `None`.

title: A data type determines how a value behaves.
body: In Python, the number 3 and the string '3' may look similar on the screen, but they behave differently. The number 3 is used in addition operations, while the string '3' can be concatenated like any other character. True and False are boolean values frequently used in conditional statements. When reading code as a beginner, don’t just look at the appearance of a value; check whether it’s enclosed in quotes, whether it’s the result of a comparison, or whether it’s used in a numerical calculation. This sidebar isn’t meant as a hint to quickly spot problems, but rather as reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial value of a variable, the value after assignment, the result of a condition, changes during a loop, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the entire code at once; instead, start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. Reading data types means predicting what actions a value can perform. Strings are good for concatenation and slicing, numbers are used for calculations, and lists hold multiple values in order. Even values that look the same can produce different results depending on their data types. When reading code, it’s helpful to highlight both the current data type of a value and any lines containing conversion functions.
detail: Data types determine how values behave. Although the number 3 and the string '3' may look similar on the screen, they are treated differently in calculations and when used in operations. When reading code, you must check for quotation marks, conversion functions, the results of comparison expressions, and whether the value is contained in a container such as a list or dictionary to reliably predict the outcome. Even if values appear identical, different data types can lead to different calculation results and varying probabilities of errors.

title: A conditional statement evaluates the result of the conditional expression first.
body: When reading an `if` statement, don’t start with the indented lines; first determine whether the condition is `True` or `False`. If the condition is `True`, the `if` block is executed; if it is `False`, the `else` block is executed if present. If there are `elif` clauses, they are evaluated in order from the top, and only the first block that evaluates to `True` is executed. If you assume that all blocks will be executed, it’s easy to get the output or variable results wrong. This sidebar isn’t meant as a hint to quickly solve problems, but rather as a reading exercise designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which code is read. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial variable value, the value after assignment, the result of the condition, changes during loops, and the final output line will reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by marking whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. In conditional statements, the result of the conditional expression is evaluated first. If the condition is True, the code inside the `if` block is executed; if it is False, the program proceeds to the `else` block or the next line. Since the conditional expression can contain comparisons, function calls, or variables themselves, it’s a good idea to first substitute actual values into it. It’s also important to note that only indented lines are affected by the conditional statement.
detail: A conditional statement first determines whether a condition is True or False, and then selects the block to execute. If the statement contains `if`, `elif`, and `else` clauses, they are evaluated from top to bottom, and only the first block that evaluates to True is executed. Since only indented lines are affected by the conditional statement, displaying both the result of the condition and the scope of the indentation helps reduce errors.

title: It's easier to understand loops by looking at a table that shows how values change with each iteration.
body: A loop is a structure that executes a single line of code multiple times. In cumulative code like `total = total + n`, the value of `total` changes with each iteration. When solving a problem, you can write down the loop counter, the value of `n`, and the value of `total` after each iteration in a table. With a `while` loop, you must pay particular attention to when the condition becomes `False`. If there is no update line like `i = i + 1`, the loop may never end. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather a guide designed to help beginners internalize the proper order for reading code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial variable values, values after assignment, the result of the condition, changes during the loop, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When you’re confused, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by noting whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. It’s easier to understand loops by creating a table showing the values that change with each iteration. Writing down loop variables like `i` or `x`, cumulative variables like `total`, and lists like `result` separately helps clarify the flow. In particular, since `range` does not include the end value, it’s helpful to get into the habit of writing down the actual numbers being iterated over first.
detail: A loop is a structure that tracks how values change as the same code is executed multiple times. If you list the loop counter, loop variable, cumulative variable, and list state in a table, the flow becomes clear. Since `range` does not include the end value and `while` stops only when the condition is `False`, you must first verify the actual number of iterations.

title: List indices start at 0.
when_to_show: When you see expressions like items[0] and items[1]
body: List indices start at 0. This card is not a review of the entire list, but rather a reading note intended to help beginners avoid common misunderstandings, particularly when reading indices. People often refer to it as “the first one,” but in a Python list, the first value is at index 0. Therefore, `items[0]` is the first value, and `items[1]` is the second value. If you interpret `items[1]` as the number 1, or mistake the second position for the first, you’ll easily get the wrong answer. Since `append` adds a new value to the end of the list, the list length increases and the last value changes. When `pop` is used, a value is removed, which can shift the positions of the remaining elements. When solving problems, it’s helpful to write the current list on one line and add indices like 0, 1, 2 below it. Then, when you see lines that access the list like `items[0]`, `items[1]`, or `items[-1]`, read the value at the current position. After using `append` or `pop`, do not rely on the old index table; update it accordingly. If `i` is used as an index in a loop, you must consider both the current value of `i` and the current state of the list. Since `len(items) - 1` is an expression used to calculate the last position, the result will change if the list length changes. This card is not meant to provide a quick hint but to help you internalize the correct order for reading code. If you distinguish whether the current line is creating a value, modifying a value, or outputting a value, you’ll make fewer mistakes even when `list`, `index`, and `append` appear together. When practicing, create a table below the list with index numbers, and redraw the table every time `append` or `pop` is executed. Indicate separately whether the value has changed, the position has changed, or the length has changed. Finally, check the outputted value and the remaining values in the entire list separately. Doing so reduces mistakes caused by mixing up position numbers and actual values.
detail: Unlike human numbering, list indices start at 0. `items[0]` is the first value, and `items[1]` is the second value. Since the list length and positions may change after calling `append` or `pop`, you should not rely on the previous position table. Check the values, positions, and length separately.

title: A dictionary looks up entries by key, not by location.
when_to_show: When you see an expression like `data['name']`,
body: Dictionaries are looked up by key, not by position. This card is a study note for beginners who confuse list indices with dictionary keys. In a list, `items[0]` refers to the 0th position, but in a dictionary, `data['age']` refers to the key named “age.” Therefore, `data['score'] = 90` does not mean inserting 90 at the “score” position; rather, it stores the value 90 under the “score” key or updates the existing value. Attempting to access a nonexistent key directly using square brackets can cause an error, whereas using `get()` allows for safe handling with a default value when the key is missing. When solving problems, look at the initial list of keys in the dictionary and mark whether each line adds a new key, updates the value of an existing key, or simply reads the value. In particular, if a key is passed as a variable inside a loop—such as `data[name] = count`—you must calculate what the actual key will be. If written as `data.get(name, 0)`, the current value of the `name` variable is a candidate for the key, and if the key does not exist, a default value like 0 is used. You must also verify whether the key is a string, a number, or a variable. Since '1' and 1 can be different keys, do not assume they are the same based solely on their apparent values. This card is not meant to provide hints for guessing the correct answer, but rather to help you master the order in which to read the code. By categorizing each line into whether it creates a value, updates a value, or outputs a value, you can reliably solve dict problems. When practicing, write potential keys on the left and value changes on the right, updating them for each line number. In particular, if the same key appears twice or more, the last assignment is likely to be the final value. Also, mark separately whether the code throws an error when a key is missing or uses a default value with `get`. Reading the code this way makes the dictionary look less like a simple box and more like a table where values are retrieved by name.
detail: A dictionary looks up values by key name, not by position. data['age'] retrieves the value associated with the key "age," while data['score'] = 90 stores or updates the value associated with the key "score." Since accessing a nonexistent key using square brackets can cause an error, you should also check whether to use `get` and whether to use a default value.

title: A function is not defined; it is executed when it is called.
when_to_show: def와 함수 호출이 함께 있을 때
body: `def` is the code used to define a function, and the function body is executed when the function is called. When `add(2, 3)` is called, 2 and 3 are passed as parameters, and the return value is sent back to the calling location. If `result = add(2, 3)`, the return value is stored in `result`. If there is only a function definition and no call, the `print` statement inside the function will not execute. The key to solving function problems is to read the definition line and the call line separately. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather a reading exercise designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial values of variables, values after assignment, the results of conditions, changes during loops, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When you’re confused, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by marking whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. A function executes when it is called, not when it is defined. The `def` line prepares the function, and actual execution begins on the line with parentheses, such as `name()`. If there are arguments, they are passed as parameters inside the function; if there is a `return` statement, the result is returned to the calling location. You should also check whether the result of the call is stored in a variable or printed immediately.
detail: A function is not executed immediately on the `def` line, but rather when it is called. Consider the function definition and the call line separately, and trace the flow: the arguments are passed as parameters, and the return value is sent back to the point of call. The meaning of the subsequent code changes depending on whether the result of the call is stored in a variable or printed immediately.

title: The `return` statement returns the function's result and terminates the function.
when_to_show: When there are multiple `return` statements in a function
body: A `return` statement returns a value to the outside of the function. Once a `return` is executed, the rest of the function body is no longer executed. If there is a `return` inside an `if` statement and the condition is `True`, the function may end at that `return`. Therefore, in function problems, you must identify which `return` is actually executed. `print` and `return` are different. `print` displays output on the screen, while `return` returns a value to the caller. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial variable values, values after assignment, the result of conditions, changes during loops, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. `return` returns the result of a function and terminates the function. Its position is important because code below `return` may not be executed. If the result of a function call is stored in a variable, subsequent lines use that return value. Unlike `print`, `return` should be understood not as displaying something on the screen, but as passing a value back to the caller.
detail: The `return` statement returns the function's result to the calling location and terminates the function's execution. Even if there is code below the `return` statement, execution will not proceed further once that `return` is executed. Since `print` displays output on the screen and `return` passes a value, in function problems, you must identify which `return` statement is actually executed.

title: Variables inside a function and variables outside a function are treated as separate scopes.
when_to_show: When a variable with the same name appears within a function
body: Variables inside a function and variables outside a function are distinguished by their scope. This card is a light, easy-to-read note that explains scope primarily through the lens of execution flow, so that beginners encountering the concept for the first time don’t find it too difficult. Variables created inside a function are typically values used mainly while the function is executing. Even if a variable inside a function has the same name as an outer variable, you shouldn’t assume that an assignment inside the function will always change the outer value. To pass a value out of a function, you typically use the `return` statement. When `return` is used, the result is sent back to the calling location, and that result can be stored in another variable. Conversely, if a function only performs calculations without using `return`, that value is difficult to use directly from outside the function. When reading a problem, write down the state separately for “before the call,” “inside the function,” and “after the call.” Before the call, identify the outer variables; inside the function, track the parameters and local variables; and after the call, verify whether the return value has been stored. If there is a `print` statement, also note the values displayed on the screen. When a name created inside a function matches a name created outside, do not treat them as a single entity; instead, distinguish which scope the name belongs to. This card is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but a tool to help you internalize the proper order for reading code. If you clearly indicate whether the current line creates a value, modifies a value, outputs to the screen, or returns a value to the caller, you’ll reduce scope errors. When practicing, create separate tables for outside the function and inside the function, and treat each call as creating a new table. Write the actual arguments in the “parameter” column, then update the local variables from top to bottom. Finally, verify the values by dividing them into three columns: the value displayed on screen, the returned value, and the value remaining in the outer variable. Doing this makes it less confusing to distinguish which scope a value belongs to, even if the names are the same.
detail: You should not assume that variables inside a function and variables outside it have the same value, even if they have the same name. You should list the outer variable before the call, the function’s parameters and local variables, and the value stored in `return` after the call separately. Dividing the values into three columns—those displayed by `print`, the returned value, and the value remaining in the outer variable—will help reduce scope errors.

title: String methods create new strings or lists.
when_to_show: When looking at split, strip, and join
body: String methods are frequently used to manipulate, split, or concatenate text. `strip` removes leading and trailing whitespace or line breaks, `split` splits a string into a list, and `join` concatenates a list of strings into a single string. Don’t assume that the original string itself changes automatically; instead, check which variable stores the result. You must reassign it—like `text = text.strip()`—for the updated value to remain in `text`. This sidebar is not meant as a hint to quickly solve problems, but rather as reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial value of a variable, the value after assignment, the result of a condition, changes during a loop, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When you’re confused, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; start by noting whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. String methods often create new strings or lists rather than modifying the original directly. `split` creates a list, `strip` creates a new, trimmed string, and `replace` returns a new, modified string. When reading code, you should check whether the method’s result is stored in a variable, compared directly, or passed to another function.
detail: String methods often return a new string or list rather than modifying the original directly. `strip` returns a trimmed string, `split` returns a list, and `replace` returns a modified string. You must check whether the result is stored back in a variable, used directly in a comparison, or passed to another function.

title: A boolean value acts as the gatekeeper in a conditional statement.
body: A boolean value is either True or False. The comparison expression `score >= 60` also produces a boolean value. Code such as `if active:` executes the `if` block if the value of `active` is evaluated as True. In boolean problems, you must distinguish whether the word “True” is being printed or used as a condition. Although the boolean used in a condition may not be visible on the screen, it determines which blocks are executed. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which code is read. Even with short code, breaking it down into the variable’s initial value, its value after assignment, the result of the condition, changes during loops, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. A `bool` value acts as the gatekeeper of a conditional statement. If it’s `True`, the inner code executes; if it’s `False`, the code is skipped or proceeds to the `else` block. The result of a comparison is also a boolean, and there are cases where the value itself behaves as if it were False, such as an empty string or an empty list. When reading code, you must first determine whether the value inside the conditional statement is actually True or False.
detail: A boolean value is either True or False and acts as a gatekeeper in conditional statements. Comparison expressions also produce boolean values, and there are values—such as an empty string or an empty list—that are evaluated as False. When reading a conditional statement, don’t look at the inner code first; instead, determine whether the value in the condition is actually True or False.

title: Error handling is a flow that wraps lines that may fail.
body: Code that might fail is placed inside the `try` block. Converting a string that is difficult to convert to a number—such as `int('x')`—can raise a `ValueError`, and if that error is caught by `except ValueError`, the `except` block is executed. Error handling isn’t a trick to get the right answer; it’s a mechanism that allows the program to continue along a different path rather than stopping immediately. Read the code separately for normal and failure cases. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly solving problems, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial value of a variable, the value after assignment, the result of a condition, changes during a loop, and the final output line will reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. Error handling is a flow that wraps lines that might fail. If a problem occurs inside a `try` block, control flows to the `except` block; if there’s no problem, the normal flow continues. When reading code, you should check what errors are anticipated and what values are used as substitutes in case of failure. Error handling is not a mechanism for hiding errors, but rather a tool for dividing the flow of execution.
detail: Error handling is a structure where lines that might fail are placed within a `try` block, and if a problem occurs, the flow is redirected to the `except` block. You need to read the code while distinguishing between the normal flow and the failure flow. Simply check what errors are expected, what values are used as replacements in case of failure, and whether errors are hidden or reported.

title: File operations are viewed as a sequence of open, read/write, and close operations.
body: File operations follow a flow where you open a file, read from or write to it, and close it when you’re done. The `with open(...) as f:` construct helps you handle this process safely. `read` reads the file’s contents as a string, and `write` writes a string to the file. Since screen output and file writing are different, you shouldn’t assume that `f.write('hi')` will print “hi” to the screen. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly debugging problems, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which code is read. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial value of a variable, its value after assignment, the result of a condition, changes during a loop, and the final output line will reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. When working with files, view the code as a flow of opening, reading or writing, and closing. If the code uses the `with open(...) as f` syntax, the file is automatically closed when the block ends. The meaning of the following code changes depending on whether the read value is a string, a list of lines, or parsed as JSON. When solving file-handling problems, you must distinguish between screen output and file storage.
detail: File operations are viewed as a sequence of opening, reading or writing, and closing. The `with open` structure helps ensure that the file is safely closed when the block ends. `read` and `write` differ from screen output; the meaning of the following code depends on whether the read value is a string, a list of lines, or the result of JSON parsing.

title: Object code distinguishes between design specifications and actual values.
body: A class is a blueprint, and an object is the actual instance created by instantiating the class. `self` refers to the current object on which the method is being executed. `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when the object is first created. When reading code as a beginner, rather than trying to memorize object-oriented concepts in depth, simply follow the sequence: class definition, object creation, attribute storage, and method invocation. This sidebar is not a hint for quickly guessing the answer to a problem, but rather reading material designed to help beginners internalize the actual order in which they should read code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial values of variables, values after assignment, the results of conditions, changes during loops, and the final output line will help reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; instead, start by identifying whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. When reading object-oriented code, you must distinguish between the design and the actual values. A `class` is a framework that defines what properties and behaviors an object can have, while an `object` or `instance` is the actual value created within that framework. Code with a dot, such as `obj.name`, represents the flow of using properties or functions within an object. Remember that even something that looks like a single variable can have an internal state.
detail: When reading object code, you must distinguish between the “class” blueprint and the actual instance created from that blueprint. The `__init__` method initializes the attributes, and `self` refers to the current object. Expressions with a dot, such as `obj.name`, represent the flow of using attributes or functions within the object, so you should also observe changes in its internal state.

title: Solve mixed-type problems by breaking them down into a checklist.
body: Mixed-type problems are difficult if you try to recall all the relevant grammar at once. First, identify the output line, then trace back to the variables or function calls required to produce that output. Next, if there are conditional statements, select only the blocks that are actually executed; if there are loops, note how the values change with each iteration. For lists and dictionaries, check the final remaining values. Simply following this checklist will significantly reduce mistakes on beginner-level problems. This sidebar is not meant as a hint for solving problems quickly, but rather as a guide to help beginners internalize the proper order for reading code. Even with short code, breaking it down into the initial variable values, values after assignment, the results of conditions, changes during loops, and the final output line will reduce mistakes. When in doubt, don’t try to memorize the whole thing at once; start by marking whether the current line creates a value, changes a value, or outputs a value. For mixed problems, breaking them down using a checklist leads to more reliable solutions. First, examine the input and initial variables; next, the condition evaluation; then, changes during loops; followed by the results of function calls; and finally, the output. It’s more important to verify where values actually change and where they are stored than to correctly identify syntax terms.
detail: When dealing with mixed problems, it’s more reliable to break them down into a checklist rather than trying to recall all the grammar terms at once. Track the sequence in the following order: initial values, values after assignment, condition checks, changes during loops, results of function calls, and final output. The key is to verify where values change and where they are retained, rather than focusing on the grammar terms themselves.
